authoredPrompt: This figure shows two fragments of a recursion tree side by side, labeled (a) and (b), with nodes carrying subproblem sizes. In (a) a top node labeled n has two branches: the left ends at a bare 0 with no box drawn around it, the right at a node labeled n-1. A large pale gray ellipse encloses the top node and the n-1 node together, and a heavy dotted arrow runs from that ellipse rightward to the expression Theta(n). The n-1 node branches in turn to two gray rectangles reading (n-1)/2 - 1 and (n-1)/2. In (b) a single node labeled n is ringed by a small pale gray ellipse, again with a dotted arrow pointing right to Theta(n), and it branches to two gray rectangles that both read (n-1)/2. The shared Theta(n) tag is the point of the comparison: the shaded groupings cost the same in each panel, while the boxed subproblems still waiting differ. Putting a lopsided split followed by an even one beside a single even split motivates the argument that alternating bad and good partitions costs about what uninterrupted good partitioning would.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between the alternating bad-good split and the balanced split: the shaded Theta(n) cost group stays comparable while the remaining subproblem boxes change, making clear why the two fragments can have similar level cost.
- Button for expanding the next recursion level: each press reveals the children produced by the current split and updates the accumulated cost label, making clear how partition balance controls the shape of the recursion tree.
- Click for a shaded ellipse: the nodes included in that Theta(n) grouping brighten together, making clear which partitioning work is being counted as one level of cost.
authoredContext:
In the average case, PARTITION produces a mix of “good” and “bad” splits. In a recursion tree for an average-case execution of PARTITION, the good and bad splits are distributed randomly throughout the tree. Suppose, for the sake of intuition, that the good and bad splits alternate levels in the tree, and that the good splits are best-case splits and the bad splits are worst-case splits. Figure 7.5(a) shows the splits at two consecutive levels in the recursion tree. At the root of the tree, the cost is n for partitioning, and the subarrays produced have sizes n 1 and 0: the worst case. At the next level, the subarray of size n 1 undergoes best-case partitioning into subarrays of size .n 1/=2 1 and .n 1/=2. Let’s assume that the boundary-condition cost is 1 for the subarray of size 0. The combination of the bad split followed by the good split produces three subarrays of sizes 0, .n  1/=2  1, and .n  1/=2 at a combined partitioning cost
of ‚.n/ C ‚.n  1/ D ‚.n/. Certainly, this situation is no worse than that in
Figure 7.5(b), namely a single level of partitioning that produces two subarrays of
size .n  1/=2, at a cost of ‚.n/. Yet this latter situation is balanced! Intuitively,
the ‚.n  1/ cost of the bad split can be absorbed into the ‚.n/ cost of the good
split, and the resulting split is good. Thus, the running time of quicksort, when levels alternate between good and bad splits, is like the running time for good splits
alone: still O.n lg n/, but with a slightly larger constant hidden by the O-notation.
We shall give a rigorous analysis of the expected running time of a randomized
version of quicksort in Section 7.4.2.

discrepancies: Gray-box labels like '(n−1)/2 − 1' and '(n−1)/2' render very small at inline size (font-size 15 in a 1200-wide viewbox), making them hard to read compared to the clearly legible boxes in the source
In panel (a) the dotted Θ(n) arrow is drawn high (y≈88, near the top of the ellipse) instead of emerging from the right-middle of the tilted ellipse as in the source
An extra level-3 row of '≈(n−1)/4' boxes is added on expand that does not appear in the source figure (a pedagogical extension, but content beyond the original)
The drawn figure is compressed into the left ~60% of the canvas with a large empty band, so the side-by-side (a)/(b) composition reads more cramped than the source's balanced two-panel layout
evaluation.notes: The recursion-tree topology, tilted enclosing ellipse, gray subproblem boxes, dotted Θ(n) arrows, and (a)/(b) split are all faithfully reproduced and the focus/expand/highlight interactions are functional and on-concept, but the sub-box labels are too small to read comfortably at inline size and the panel-(a) arrow placement and overall composition deviate slightly from the source.
action_items: Increase the font size of the gray-box labels (and node labels) so '(n−1)/2 − 1' etc. are comfortably legible at inline rendering, e.g. raise box text to ~20-22 in the 1200 viewbox or shrink the viewbox to fit content tighter.
Move the panel-(a) dotted arrow down so it originates from the right-middle of the tilted ellipse (around the n−1 node height) rather than near the top, matching the source.
Tighten the viewbox or scale the drawing so panels (a) and (b) fill the available width more evenly and reduce the large empty right band.
